Analyzing and Reporting Simulation Results

Source: vignettes/analyzing-results.qmd

Overview

medsim_run() returns a medsim_results object. This article covers what that object holds, which analysis function answers which question, how to compare methods fairly, and how to turn the results into tables and figures.

The examples continue the Sobel study from Tutorial: Your First Coverage Study: two scenarios (“Medium”, ab=.1521ab = .1521; “Null (a = 0)”, ab=0ab = 0), 500 replications each.

Question Function Needs from the method
Is the estimator biased or noisy? medsim_analyze() <param> + truth
Bias, empirical SE and model SE, with MCSEs medsim_analyze_performance() <param>, <param>_se + truth
Do the intervals cover? medsim_analyze_coverage() <param>_ci_lower, <param>_ci_upper + truth
How often does the test reject? medsim_analyze_power() <param>_p
Which method is better? medsim_compare_methods() two or more runs on the same scenarios
How many replications? medsim_nsim_for_mcse() nothing (planning)

The results object 

names(results)
#> [1] "results"     "summary"     "truth"       "config"      "scenarios"
#> [6] "method_name" "timestamp"
  • results$results holds one row per scenario × replication: the method’s outputs, plus scenario, replication, elapsed (seconds) and error (NA when the replication succeeded).
  • results$truth holds one row per scenario: the values returned by compute_truth.
  • results$config and results$scenarios record how the run was made, so a saved results file documents itself.

Failed replications are kept, not dropped. Count them before you analyze:

tapply(!is.na(results$results$error), results$results$scenario, sum)

The coverage table reports these as n_failed and failure_rate. A method that fails selectively (for example, on hard data sets) can look better than it is if the failures are ignored.

Accuracy: medsim_analyze() 

an <- medsim_analyze(results)
an$by_scenario[, c("scenario", "parameter", "bias", "rmse", "relative_bias")]
#>       scenario parameter          bias       rmse relative_bias
#> 1       Medium  indirect  0.0013953010 0.03928207     0.9173576
#> 2 Null (a = 0)  indirect -0.0008496464 0.02809685            NA

relative_bias is in percent of the true value. It is NA where the truth is zero, so report absolute bias for null scenarios.

medsim_analyze() scores every output column that has a matching truth value. It skips SE, interval and p-value columns (indirect_se, indirect_ci_lower, indirect_ci_upper, indirect_p) silently, because they belong to a scored estimate. Any other output column without a truth is named in a single warning, so a value you forgot to return from compute_truth is still flagged.

Performance with Monte Carlo SEs

Every number in a simulation table is itself an estimate. Morris, White and Crowther (2019) recommend reporting each with its Monte Carlo SE (MCSE). medsim_analyze_performance() does that for bias, and compares the method’s own SE with the empirical SD of its estimates:

perf <- medsim_analyze_performance(results)
perf
#>       scenario parameter          bias   bias_mcse empirical_se   model_se
#> 1       Medium  indirect  0.0013953010 0.001757397   0.03929660 0.03969967
#> 2 Null (a = 0)  indirect -0.0008496464 0.001257212   0.02811212 0.02846886
#>         rmse n_converged n_failed
#> 1 0.03928207         500        0
#> 2 0.02809685         500        0

Read bias against bias_mcse. Here both biases are under one MCSE, so there is no detectable bias. A model_se well below empirical_se means the method’s standard errors are too small, which usually shows up as under-coverage.

Coverage and rejection rates 

cov <- medsim_analyze_coverage(results, ci_levels = 0.95)
pw  <- medsim_analyze_power(results, alpha = 0.05)

Coverage reports its own MCSE (coverage_mcse). For a rejection rate pp estimated from RR replications, the MCSE is p(1−p)/R\sqrt{p(1-p)/R}. At the nominal .05 and R=500R = 500 that is about .0097, so a type I error between roughly .03 and .07 is consistent with a correct test.

How many replications?

Invert the MCSE formula when you plan a study. To estimate 95% coverage with an MCSE of .005:

medsim_nsim_for_mcse(target_mcse = 0.005, p = 0.95)
#> [1] 1900

Plan for the worst case you need to resolve. A rejection rate near .5 has the largest MCSE, so power studies need more replications than coverage studies at the same precision.

Comparing methods fairly

Run each method on the same scenario list and pass the results to medsim_compare_methods():

mc <- function(data, params) {
  fm <- summary(lm(M ~ X, data = data))$coefficients
  fy <- summary(lm(Y ~ X + M, data = data))$coefficients
  ab <- rnorm(5000, fm["X", 1], fm["X", 2]) * rnorm(5000, fy["M", 1], fy["M", 2])
  q  <- quantile(ab, c(0.025, 0.975), names = FALSE)
  list(indirect = fm["X", 1] * fy["M", 1],
       indirect_ci_lower = q[1], indirect_ci_upper = q[2])
}
results_mc <- medsim_run(mc, scenarios, config, compute_truth = truth)

medsim_compare_methods(sobel = results, mc = results_mc)
#> Accuracy Comparison:
#>  method parameter        mae      rmse         bias
#>   sobel  indirect 0.02630142 0.0341505 0.0002728273
#>     mc  indirect 0.02630142 0.0341505 0.0002728273
#> ...
#> Coverage Comparison:
#>  method parameter coverage n_valid
#>   sobel  indirect    0.952    1000
#>     mc  indirect    0.945    1000

The two accuracy rows are identical, and that is by design. Both methods report the same point estimate âb̂\hat a \hat b, and medsim seeds each replication from the scenario name and replication number, so both methods saw exactly the same 1,000 data sets. This pairing (common random numbers) means differences between methods are not diluted by data-set noise. The comparison above isolates the interval: the Monte Carlo CI covers .945 against Sobel’s .952 on identical data.

Keep scenario names fixed

Pairing holds only when the scenario names and replication numbers match. Renaming a scenario between runs breaks it silently.

Tables

Each medsim_table_*() function takes an analysis object and returns LaTeX. medsim_write_table() writes it to disk, with the format inferred from the file extension:

tab <- medsim_table_coverage(cov, expected = 0.95,
                             caption = "Sobel CI coverage")
medsim_write_table(tab, "tables/coverage.tex")

medsim_table_power(pw)
medsim_table_accuracy(an, metrics = c("bias", "rmse"))

medsim_tables(results, output_dir = "tables") writes the standard set (accuracy, coverage, power) in one call.

Figures

The plotting functions return ggplot2 objects, so you can restyle them:

medsim_plot_coverage(cov, expected_coverage = 0.95, tolerance = 0.02)
medsim_plot_error_boxplot(results, parameter = "indirect")

medsim_figures(results, output_dir = "figures") writes the standard set as PDFs.

Everything at once

medsim_workflow() runs the analysis and writes all standard tables and figures:

medsim_workflow(results, output_dir = "results")
list.files("results", recursive = TRUE)
#> [1] "figures/coverage.pdf"      "figures/error_boxplot.pdf"
#> [3] "figures/timing.pdf"        "tables/table_accuracy.tex"
#> [5] "tables/table_coverage.tex" "tables/table_power.tex"

Use it for a first look. For a manuscript, call the individual functions so you control captions, labels and which parameters appear.

Reference

Morris, T. P., White, I. R., & Crowther, M. J. (2019). Using simulation studies to evaluate statistical methods. Statistics in Medicine, 38(11), 2074–2102. https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.8086
